title: Galaxy Cluster Abell 2218’s “Gravitational Lens”
caption: The galaxy cluster Abell 2218, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: Abell 2218 · constellation Draco · about 2 billion light-years away (source figure)
credit: NASA, ESA, Richard Ellis (Caltech) and Jean-Paul Kneib (Observatoire Midi-Pyrenees, France); Acknowledgment: NASA, A. Fruchter and the ERO Team (STScI and ST-ECF)

recognition.text: NASA Hubble image release (STScI). No published audience rating.

story: This Hubble view looks into Abell 2218, a rich cluster of thousands of galaxies about 2 billion light-years away in the constellation Draco. Its total mass is equivalent to ten thousand galaxies, and that huge concentration of matter bends and magnifies light from galaxies far behind it, as Einstein's general theory of relativity predicts. Lenses like this act as natural magnifying glasses, letting astronomers study galaxies too faint to detect otherwise.

A team led by Richard Ellis of Caltech used Abell 2218 in exactly that way, working with Hubble and the Keck Telescopes in Hawaii. They found a very small, faint galaxy about 13.4 billion light-years away, magnified more than 30 times by the cluster and split into two images by the uneven spread of matter within it. It is only around 500 light-years across and holds just a few million times the Sun's mass.
The team thinks it is possibly one of the building blocks that later join to make larger galaxies, and that it may show the conditions in which the first generation of stars formed.

understand.summary: Hubble's Wide Field Planetary Camera 2 took the image. The colour mapping is not published.
understand.eye: Some 9.4 hours of exposure gather light from galaxies far too faint for the eye, and the cluster's lensing brightens some of them further.

explore: Without the lens, Ellis said, the galaxy would not have shown up even in the Hubble Deep Fields. At the time, NASA expected its planned Next Generation Space Telescope to use lenses like this one to look back toward the very first objects in the universe.
sources: NASA release: Gravitational Lens Helps Hubble and Keck Discover Galaxy Building Block
